The warning is contained in the UNFPA’s 2026 State of World Population report, titled Succeeding Generations: Empowering Young People to Chart the Future, released on Thursday. Drawing on a survey of more than 108,000 internet-connected young adults aged eighteen to thirty-nine across seventy-three countries and territories, the report challenges the perception that younger generations are increasingly turning away from marriage and parenthood. It found that seventy per cent of respondents considered marriage their ideal relationship arrangement, while 91 per cent wanted at least one child. However, economic difficulties are making it increasingly difficult for many to realise those aspirations. According to the report, financial insecurity was identified as the most commonly reported obstacle to finding a partner by fifty-seven per cent of respondents, while seventy-two per cent said it was a barrier to having children. The findings also showed that more than forty per cent of respondents aged 35 to 39 who considered marriage their ideal relationship arrangement were unmarried. The report further revealed that one in five young people globally were not in employment, education or training, while four in five young adults in low-income countries lacked secure paid employment. UNFPA Executive Director, Diene Keita, said young people were increasingly finding it difficult to secure the basic conditions needed to build the lives they wanted. “Young people want independence, stable relationships, and many want children. But too often, economic insecurity, unaffordable housing, conflict and exclusion are putting those aspirations out of reach,” she said. Keita called for greater investment in young people’s health, education and economic opportunities, stressing the need to turn their ambitions into real choices. The report identified sub-Saharan Africa as a region facing particular challenges, with limited employment opportunities and rapid population growth adding pressure on governments. It cited youth unemployment rates of more than 35 per cent in Senegal and 30 per cent in Mali in 2024. The findings also highlighted the difficulties confronting girls in the region, including poverty, child marriage and adolescent pregnancy, which continue to limit access to education. In Benin, only about one in three girls completes the first cycle of secondary education, while in Chad, more than 60 per cent of women were married before the age of 18. Nigeria, however, recorded progress in girls’ education, with secondary school completion rates rising by a quarter between 2018 and 2024, according to the report. UNFPA said investments in free schooling, school meals and safe spaces had also contributed to declining child marriage rates. Beyond economic pressures, the report identified conflict, climate change, technological disruption and inequality as factors shaping young people’s transition into adulthood. It noted that the number of people aged ten to twenty-four living within fifty kilometres of active conflict more than doubled from 164 million in 1990 to 340 million in 2022. The report urged governments and development partners to improve access to decent employment, affordable housing, education, healthcare and social protection, while ensuring young people have a meaningful role in decisions affecting their future. It argued that enabling young people to build secure lives and families should be treated as an investment in future generations, rather than reducing demographic debates to concerns about birth rates.
